newsitem.title: CHINA: China urban jobless rate soaring - economist.
newsitem.headline: China urban jobless rate soaring - economist.

text.p: China's real jobless rate is much higher than official figures reveal and Beijing must boost jobs in the services and private sectors to prevent social instability, according to a senior Chinese economist.

China's official urban jobless rate -- which stood at 3.0 percent at the end of 1996 -- only counted registered unemployed while ignoring huge numbers of redundant workers, most languishing in state firms, Hu Angang, a senior researcher with the Chinese Academy of Sciences, said in a paper made available to Reuters.

China's real urban jobless rate was 7.5 percent based on 1996 data if redundant workers -- or those sent home from their jobs on just a fraction of their former salaries while remaining on formal payrolls -- were counted, Hu said.
"This shows that China's problem of urban unemployment is growing more and more pronounced, and its effects on social stability are becoming more and more serious," Hu wrote.
Unemployment was at one of the highest levels since the communists took power in 1949, including many jobless laid off from ailing state and collective enterprises, Hu said.
Rising unemployment was casting a shadow over rural areas, with figures for 1995 showing 175 million farmers -- or 48.7 percent of the rural labour force -- were surplus, he said.
The problem was worsening even though tens of millions of surplus farm workers have abandoned their hoes and sought their fortunes in cities, he said.

To find work for the swelling ranks of idle and jobless workers, China should abandon its commitment to propping up the wheezing state sector in favour of nurturing more nimble and market-responsive private and small-scale businesses, he said.

China's communist rulers have been reluctant to reform the lumbering state sector for fear that huge numbers of jobless could spark social unrest and spell an end to party rule, and amid concerns that the state-owned sector could lose its dominant role.
"State-owned collectives and some urban collective enterprises are growing at quite a rapid pace, but compared with non-state enterprises... they don't have competitive advantages," he said.
"Existence (of non-state business) is based on the functions of the market and is not a result of direct government intervention," he said.
Authorities should grant non-state and small businesses the same preferential policies Beijing used to help big state firms, he said, citing this as a means of creating more jobs.
"The government is now focusing on large and medium-sized enterprises, which is correct, but at the same time it should also actively develop small enterprises," Hu said.

Beijing should try to spur growth in services such as food, trade, tourism and social work, he said, adding that such industries had absorbed five million workers a year in the 1980s and more than 10 million a year from 1990-1995.
"The main way for solving China's high urban jobless rate is by developing employment channels for tertiary industries and urging workers in manufacturing to move to tertiary industries," he said.
Hu estimated the real number of unemployed at about 15 million. China's urban workforce was an estimated 198 million people at the end of 1996, he said.
